analysis.one_liner: Adds prison time for illegal robocalls and doubles fines for fake caller ID.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill that would have sent willful robocallers to prison for up to three years and doubled spoofed-caller-ID fines to $20,000 sat in a House subcommittee for two years and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The DO NOT Call Act would make it a federal crime to knowingly break the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, the law against unwanted automated calls and texts. First-time offenders could face up to a year in prison, and repeat offenders, mass callers, or scammers causing $5,000 or more in losses could face up to three years [S2][S3]. It would also double the fine for faking caller ID information from $10,000 to $20,000 [S2][S3]. The bill never advanced past a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a phone who gets unwanted robocalls, spam texts, and scam calls, especially older Americans who are the main targets of phone fraud. Criminal penalties and higher fines are meant to deter the high-volume calling operations that current civil fines have not stopped [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to one year in prison, to willfully and knowingly violate the restrictions on automated telemarketing calls and messages — a step beyond the civil fines that exist today.

Adds an aggravated offense carrying up to three years in prison for repeat offenders, for operations blasting more than 100,000 calls in a day or 1,000,000 in a month, for calls made to further a felony, and for violations causing $5,000 or more in losses in a year.
Doubles the fine for knowingly transmitting misleading or inaccurate caller ID information — 'spoofing' — from $10,000 to $20,000.

analysis.who_pays: Robocall operators, spam-text senders, and telemarketers that break the automated-call rules, who would face prison exposure for the first time, plus callers who fake caller ID, who would face doubled fines. Legitimate callers who misjudge the rules could also be exposed, since criminal liability attaches to any willful violation.

drawbacks.text: Criminal liability would attach to any willful violation of the automated-call rules, and the loss trigger is low — $5,000 in aggregate harm in a year — so legitimate businesses that misjudge the Telephone Consumer Protection Act's detailed consent rules could face prosecution rather than just civil fines.

Prison terms mainly deter callers inside U.S. jurisdiction; many of the largest scam-call operations run from call centers overseas, where prosecution is difficult, so the bill would raise costs for some violators without cutting off the worst fraud at its source.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real: illegal robocalls are among the most common consumer complaints and phone scams cost Americans billions a year, and the bill targets exactly the high-volume operators that civil fines have failed to stop. The costs are modest and manageable — a good-faith carve-out could have protected legitimate callers, and offshore scammers would remain hard to reach. On balance a low-cost consumer-protection measure that died without opposition ever being aired.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee in February 2023 and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025, never getting a markup or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. David Kustoff introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, with Rep. Deborah Ross as an original cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Eight days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, which is where it stayed; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for the rest of the 118th Congress.
The bill drew 40 cosponsors split across both parties — 16 Democrats and 24 Republicans — but that support never translated into committee action or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Robocall and spam-text operations are better off, because they continue to face only civil fines rather than prison exposure; the House Energy and Commerce Committee also avoided having to act on criminal penalties for automated calling.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — a Republican sponsor with a Democratic original cosponsor, and cosponsors split 16 Democrats to 24 Republicans — and no one ever voted against it because no vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill would convert what is now a fineable offense into a federal crime carrying up to three years in prison, directly threatening the business model of high-volume automated callers. Their interest in avoiding criminal exposure runs against phone users who want the calls to stop.

The Telephone Consumer Protection Act covers texts as well as calls, so mass illegal texting would carry prison exposure for the first time. Legitimate marketers who follow the consent rules would be unaffected.
The fine for knowingly transmitting fake caller ID doubles to $20,000, raising the cost of the spoofing services that scam calls rely on.
